meta.title: The D Form, and the Ladder Up the Low E
meta.summary: The D form is the one window whose twelve dots need five frets instead of four, and the low E string, played alone, turns out to be the list of exactly where every one of the five windows begins.

spans.text: The D form of
C
sits with its barre at fret

props.caption: The same window as the roots and the triad, chapters 1 and 2 — now spread over five frets instead of four.

spans.text: Four of the five windows in this chapter pack their twelve dots into four frets. This one needs five — from
at the bottom all the way to

at the top. That's not a small difference under the hand: it's the one window in the chapter that asks for a shift, or a pinky stretch, rather than a hand that just settles in and stays. If you can't reach every dot here in one position, that's the shape talking, not your hand.
The cause is the same one chapter 1 and chapter 2 both ran into, showing up here for a third time. Five of the six strings — 6, 5, 4, 3 and 1 — put their upper dot at fret
. String 2's upper dot sits one fret higher, at fret
— the B string doing what it always does, because
G → B
is the one major third in standard tuning, where every other string pair is a fourth. That single extra fret is what turns a shape that would otherwise fit in four frets into one that needs five.
Five dots here are new since
the triad
and

and the
again. Of the five windows, this is the one with the fewest roots and fifths: only
and
are roots at all, and both sit at awkward edges of the shape rather than somewhere convenient. The D form triples the
and the
instead, so of everywhere in this chapter, this window carries the most movement and asks for the most planning if you want to land on a chord tone rather than just pass through one.

Chapter 2 called the D form the smallest of the five — a four-string fragment, never played whole. As a scale window it is the opposite: the widest of the five, not the smallest. The chord that takes the least space on the neck turns out to need the most room once its scale fills in around it.

That's the D form's own character. What's left is the fact this whole chapter has been building toward, and it starts with what happens where two windows meet. Every overlap between neighbouring windows — C and A, A and G, G and E, E and D — holds all five notes of the pentatonic, one on each string, six dots covering
complete.

So wherever you stop on this neck, the notes under your hand belong to two windows at once, and both a whole scale and a whole chord are already sitting there. Chapter 2 proved this in chord tones alone; here it's the same claim with the whole scale in it.
Here's the best single fact this chapter has to offer. Play the C major pentatonic on the low E string by itself, nothing else, and you land on frets
and
— then fret
, where it starts over. Those are exactly the five forms' barre frets, in CAGED order: C at the nut, A at
, G at
, E at
, D at
. The scale you just spent five lessons learning in five separate windows is, on one string, the list of exactly where those windows begin.

Look at the pattern in that table and it says the same thing a different way: each window's lower dot on string 6 is the upper dot of the window below it. C's top note on that string is A's bottom note; A's top is G's bottom; and so on, all the way up. The interlock chapter 2 already proved in chord tones is the same interlock here, walked up a single string.

The same five windows carry every layer this pathway adds. Chapter 4 puts the last two notes into each one, and the shape count still doesn't change — no new positions to learn, only more of what's already there. The two three-fret steps in every window you've just learned are where those two notes will land.
